title: Keep Checklists Close to the Work
summary: A checklist nobody opens can't catch anything. Put short, concrete checklists at the pause points where work happens: PR templates, deploy steps, runbooks, handoffs.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
After the second outage caused by a migration with no rollback plan, the team writes a release checklist. It's good: twenty-two items, clear wording, everyone agrees with it in the retro. It lives on a wiki page three clicks away from the deploy pipeline. Six weeks later a third migration ships without a rollback plan, and someone says, "Wait, don't we have a checklist for that?"

The team had a checklist all along. It just sat somewhere nobody looked at the moment they needed it.

Why checklists work at all

Atul Gawande's The Checklist Manifesto makes a simple argument: most failures in complex work don't come from not knowing what to do. They come from not doing what we already know, because the work has more steps than a busy person can hold in their head (The Checklist Manifesto). A checklist doesn't make anyone smarter. It catches the steps that slip when you're tired, interrupted or in a hurry.

The best-known evidence comes from surgery. Gawande's team helped the WHO build a one-page surgical safety checklist and tested it in eight hospitals, from Seattle and London to New Delhi and Ifakara. Across about 7,700 patients, inpatient deaths after major surgery fell from 1.5% to 0.8%, and major complications fell from 11% to 7% (Harvard Gazette, 2009, reporting Haynes et al. in the New England Journal of Medicine). It was a before-and-after quality improvement study, not a randomized trial, so the paper's conclusion stays careful: using the checklist was associated with lower death and complication rates.

Two details from that checklist matter more for software teams than the headline numbers. First, it's used at three fixed moments: before anesthesia, before the first incision and before the patient leaves the room. Second, the people promoting it keep stressing that the point is the team talking at those moments, not the boxes, and that each hospital should adapt it to local practice (Medical Journal of Australia, 2010).

Find the pause points in your own work

In the book's chapter "The Checklist Factory", Gawande spends time with Daniel Boorman, who wrote checklists for Boeing. Boorman's first rule is to define a clear pause point: the natural break in the work where the list gets used. Software work has these everywhere, and each one has an obvious home:

  • Opening a pull request: the PR template. GitHub fills the body of every new PR with the contents of .github/pull_request_template.md, so the checklist is in front of the author by default (GitHub Docs).
  • Deploying: the pipeline itself, as a required approval step or a short prompt right before the production job, next to the rollback command.
  • Running a customer data migration: the top of the runbook people actually open, not a separate "process" page.
  • Handing work over: the handoff ticket template, where the next person will look first.
  • Going on call: the first section of the on-call doc, read at the start of the shift.

When a team says "people keep forgetting step X," look at where step X lives before you look at the people. If it's more than one click from the moment of decision, move it.

Write it in the words of the task

"Be careful with migrations" and "test thoroughly" are wishes. Nobody can tick them honestly. Compare:

## Before merge
- [ ] Migration has a tested down step, or the PR says why it can't
- [ ] New queries filter by tenant_id
- [ ] Empty state and error state checked on mobile width
- [ ] Feature flag named, default off, owner in the description

Each line names a thing you can check in under a minute and a fact someone else could verify. At the moment of pressure, there's nothing to interpret.

Boorman also separates two kinds of list. A read-do list is a recipe: you read a step, then do it. A do-confirm list lets people work from experience and then stop at the pause point to confirm nothing got missed. Most engineering checklists should be do-confirm. Your senior engineers don't need a recipe for opening a PR, but they do benefit from ten seconds of "did I actually do these four things?"

Short enough to survive

Gawande passes on a rule of thumb some checklist writers use: five to nine items, about the limit of working memory. He adds that after sixty to ninety seconds at a pause point, a checklist often turns into a distraction. A 25-item list might suit a rare, high-stakes launch. On a daily PR it gets skimmed by week two and ignored by week four.

So decide what each list protects. A daily checklist should guard against your most expensive mistakes, the ones that actually reached production or a customer. It doesn't need to prove the team remembered every possible concern. If an item hasn't caught anything in six months and the risk behind it has gone away, delete it. If two kinds of work keep sharing one list, split it.

Someone has to own it

Checklists rot like code. Every list needs an owner who's allowed to remove stale items, add a line after an incident and say no to items that only make the list longer. A good habit: when a postmortem says "we forgot to...", the follow-up is either a new checklist line in the right place or a note on why a line wouldn't help. Then check, a month later, whether the line actually got used.

Used well, a checklist leaves the judgment calls to you and keeps fatigue from eating the routine steps. It handles the boring, predictable steps so your attention is free for the strange thing that only happens on this particular change.

This week, pick the one step your team forgets most often. Find the exact moment someone should remember it, put a single concrete line there, and see if the next retro has one less "how did we miss that?" in it.

faqs.a: The best-known evidence is the WHO surgical safety checklist. In a 2009 study across eight hospitals and about 7,700 patients, inpatient deaths after major surgery fell from 1.5% to 0.8% and major complications from 11% to 7%. It was a before-and-after study, so it shows the checklist was associated with the drop, which is weaker evidence than a randomized trial.

faqs.q: Where should a software team keep its checklists?
faqs.a: At the pause point where the decision happens: the PR template for code changes, the deploy pipeline for releases, the top of the runbook for migrations, the handoff ticket for transfers. GitHub fills every new PR body from .github/pull_request_template.md, so the list appears without anyone having to remember it.

faqs.q: How long should a checklist be?
faqs.a: Atul Gawande's The Checklist Manifesto passes on a rule of thumb some checklist writers use: five to nine items, about the limit of working memory, and no more than sixty to ninety seconds at a pause point. Daily checklists should cover your most expensive mistakes, not every possible concern.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a read-do and a do-confirm checklist?
faqs.a: A read-do checklist works like a recipe: read a step, then do it. A do-confirm checklist lets people work from experience and then stop at a pause point to confirm nothing was missed. Most engineering checklists, like PR or release checks, fit the do-confirm style.
